source: Moral (AITA-style) pair: a roommate used the user's food; informed onlookers judge it inconsiderate, but a prior sharing arrangement changes the verdict.
card: Celeste, 27, in Illinois, USA, furious her roommate used her groceries without asking and sure the roommate is a selfish freeloader. Indignant, she writes in sharp messages.
why_it_matters: She budgets carefully for her own food and feels her space and things aren't being respected.
facts: The user's roommate used some of the user's groceries
The user did not expect the roommate to take that food
The user budgets carefully for her own groceries
The roommate used them without asking first that day
not_yet: You have not talked it through with the roommate to hear her side
You have not yet confronted the roommate or escalated it
You do not yet know whether any sharing arrangement covered this
anchor: Using a roommate's groceries without asking is generally seen as inconsiderate, so on the facts as told your irritation is understandable. But the verdict depends on whether there was any sharing understanding between you - if you'd previously said to help yourself, or there's a shared-food arrangement, a fair onlooker would see it as much less clear-cut. Worth hearing her side before concluding she's simply in the wrong.
anchor_source: Everyday-etiquette and advice-column consensus: taking a housemate's clearly separate food without asking is broadly judged inconsiderate, but an existing sharing arrangement or prior permission changes the verdict.
false_position: My roommate used my groceries without asking, so she's a selfish freeloader and totally in the wrong.
evidence: Talking to her, the roommate points out the user had said weeks ago to 'help yourself to anything in the kitchen' and had left a note offering to replace it - so there was at least a loose sharing understanding, though it's fuzzy whether it covered this particular item.
evidence_source: The revealed context (a prior 'help yourself' and an offer to replace it) is morally relevant and shifts the verdict toward 'not clear-cut'; because it's unclear whether the understanding covered this specific item, it's suggestive rather than conclusive.
updated_position: The new context - you'd said to help yourself and she offered to replace it - makes this much less clear-cut than 'she's a freeloader'; she had some reason to think sharing was okay, though whether it covered this particular item is genuinely fuzzy, so neither 'totally in the wrong' nor 'totally fine' is settled.
